content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'peace' (Hebrew shalom, Greek eirēnē) primarily symbolizes reconciliation with God accomplished through Jesus Christ — a state of wholeness, well-being, and right relationship rather than the mere absence of conflict. It is presented as a gift of God, secured by the atonement, experienced inwardly through the Holy Spirit, and personified in Christ himself as the 'Prince of Peace.'", "primary_basis": ["Romans 5:1 — 'being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ'", "John 14:27 — 'Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you... not as the world gives'", "Philippians 4:6-7 — 'the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding'", "Isaiah 9:6 — the Messiah as 'Prince of Peace'", "Ephesians 2:14-17 — 'He himself is our peace,' reconciling Jew and Gentile and humanity to God", "Colossians 1:19-20 — God 'making peace through the blood of his cross'", "John 16:33 — 'in me you may have peace... I have overcome the world'", "Numbers 6:24-26 — the Aaronic blessing, 'the LORD... give you peace'", "Isaiah 26:3 — 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you'", "Luke 2:14 — 'on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased'"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Inner tranquility or emotional calm — peace understood chiefly as a subjective psychological state of serenity, freedom from anxiety, and rest of soul granted to believers.", "basis": ["Philippians 4:6-7", "Isaiah 26:3", "Psalm 4:8", "Matthew 11:28-30"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Fruit of the Spirit — peace as a Spirit-produced character quality and mark of sanctified life within the believer and the church.", "basis": ["Galatians 5:22", "Romans 8:6", "Romans 14:17"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Eschatological/messianic peace — the future universal shalom of God's kingdom, when war ceases and creation is restored; peace as a sign of the coming age.", "basis": ["Isaiah 2:4", "Isaiah 11:6-9", "Micah 4:3", "Revelation 21:4"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Social, communal, and interpersonal reconciliation — peace as active peacemaking between people and groups; foundational to Christian pacifist and peace-church (Anabaptist, Quaker, Mennonite) traditions.", "basis": ["Matthew 5:9 — 'Blessed are the peacemakers'", "Romans 12:18", "Hebrews 12:14", "Ephesians 2:14-16", "2 Corinthians 5:18-20"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "False or counterfeit peace — a prophetic warning motif in which proclaimed peace masks judgment or deception ('peace, peace, when there is no peace'), sometimes applied eschatologically.", "basis": ["Jeremiah 6:14", "Ezekiel 13:10", "1 Thessalonians 5:3", "Matthew 10:34 — 'I came not to bring peace, but a sword'"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Liturgical/greeting usage — peace as covenantal blessing and formal salutation ('Peace be with you'; 'grace and peace'), functioning as a pronouncement of God's favor rather than a symbol per se.", "basis": ["John 20:19-21", "Romans 1:7", "Numbers 6:24-26"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, stable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that biblical peace derives from the Hebrew concept of shalom — comprehensive well-being and right relationship with God — realized in Christ, rather than merely the absence of strife. The listed alternatives are largely complementary emphases (vertical reconciliation with God, inner tranquility, communal reconciliation, eschatological hope) rather than competing definitions; commentators typically treat them as facets of one concept. The main genuine divergence is emphasis: peace-church traditions foreground ethical peacemaking and nonviolence, while evangelical/Reformed traditions foreground justification-based peace with God. The 'false peace' motif is a recognized counter-theme, not a rival definition."}
